Financial metrics like gross margin reflect the impact of inventory changes on the cost of goods sold (COGS) through the relationship between inventory valuation and the cost of goods sold. When using FIFO (First-In, First-Out) inventory accounting, the oldest inventory items are sold first, and the most recent costs are assigned to ending inventory. This impacts COGS and, consequently, gross margin, which is calculated as (Revenue - COGS) / Revenue.

The matching principle states that expenses should be recognized in the same period as the related revenues. When inventory changes, the cost of goods sold is affected, and this directly influences gross margin. For example, consider a product-oriented business that sells electronics. If the business has a high inventory turnover (many units sold), the COGS will be higher, reducing gross margin. Conversely, if inventory turnover is low, COGS will be lower, increasing gross margin.

Let’s take an example: A tech company sells 10,000 smartphones in a year. The cost of manufacturing these phones was $100 each in the first quarter and $120 each in the second quarter. Using FIFO, the COGS will be $100 per unit for all 10,000 units. If the company had sold only 5,000 units in the first quarter, the remaining 5,000 units would be valued at $120, increasing COGS and reducing gross margin. This illustrates how inventory changes, under FIFO, directly affect COGS and, thus, gross margin.
